title: Six Dots That Opened a World of Books

passage.title: Six Dots That Opened a World of Books
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
In 1821, a twelve-year-old boy named Louis Braille went to a school for blind kids in Paris, France. He had lost his sight as a young child, and he was eager to read books on his own. However, the school library held only fourteen books in the entire building. Those volumes used giant raised letters pressed into thick paper coated with wax. Each book weighed twenty pounds and took minutes to trace just one sentence with a finger. Worse still, blind students had no way to write their own notes.

That year, a French army officer named Charles Barbier came to the school to share a code he called night writing. Soldiers had tried using this system of raised bumps to read battle messages in the dark without striking a match. His code used twelve raised dots set in two tall rows. While the idea excited Louis right away, the army code had a major flaw. Twelve dots were too tall to fit under one finger at once. Readers had to move their finger up and down to feel each sign.

Louis spent the next three years working late in his room to make a faster, simpler code. Using a blunt awl from his father's shop, he pressed thousands of test dots into thick paper. At age fifteen, he found the answer by cutting the tall twelve-dot cell in half. The new six-dot reading cell, arranged in two short columns of three tiny bumps, was easily felt by a reader's fingertip in a single touch. A reader could now glide smoothly across a page without stopping.

Even though each cell held only six spots, Louis found a way to make sixty-three dot shapes. The first ten letters of the alphabet used only the top four dots in the cell. The next ten letters just added one bottom dot to those first ten shapes. Other dot shapes stood for numbers, stops, and even music notes. With a metal frame called a slate and a small pointed stylus, blind students could also punch their own raised words into paper.

Today, the code known as braille is used in almost every land around the world. Raised braille cells show up on lift buttons, pill boxes, food menus, and keys. By refusing to give up on a flawed idea, a young student gave millions of blind people the power to read and write.

tier2Words.definition: individual books, especially large or heavy ones in a library collection
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin volumen, meaning 'roll of parchment or book'
tier2Words.contextClue: The school library held only fourteen books, and each of those heavy books weighed twenty pounds.

tier2Words.definition: a weakness, mistake, or design problem that keeps something from working well
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old Norse flaga, meaning 'crack or weak spot'
tier2Words.contextClue: Captain Barbier's army code had a major problem because twelve dots were too tall to fit beneath one fingertip.

tier2Words.definition: having a rounded or dull tip rather than a sharp point
tier2Words.rootHint: From Middle English blunt, meaning 'dull or not sharp'
tier2Words.contextClue: Louis used a rounded awl tool to press raised bumps into thick paper without poking holes all the way through.

tier2Words.definition: a small pen-shaped tool with a pointed tip used for pressing marks or dots into a surface
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin stilus, meaning 'pointed writing tool used on wax tablets'
tier2Words.contextClue: With a grooved metal frame and a small pointed tool, students could punch their own raised words into paper.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The new six-dot reading cell, arranged in two short columns of three tiny bumps, was easily felt by a reader's fingertip in a single touch."

Based on the structure of the sentence, what felt the new six-dot reading cell?

options.text: The two short columns felt the reader's fingertip in the dark.
A reader's fingertip felt the new six-dot reading cell in a single touch.
The three tiny bumps felt the blunt awl on the thick paper.
Captain Barbier felt the fourteen heavy wax books in the library.

questions.provingSentenceText: The new six-dot reading cell, arranged in two short columns of three tiny bumps, was easily felt by a reader's fingertip in a single touch.
questions.childTip: Find the 'by' phrase right after 'was easily felt' to see what performed the action.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'The new six-dot reading cell' receives the action, while 'by a reader's fingertip' identifies what felt the cell.

questions.prompt: According to Paragraph 1, why were the fourteen books in the Paris school library so difficult for blind students to use?

options.text: Each book weighed twenty pounds and took minutes to trace a single sentence of giant raised letters.
The books were written in a secret army code that only Captain Barbier knew how to read.
The pages were made of thin tissue paper that tore whenever a student touched them.
The school principal kept all fourteen books locked inside a leather shop across town.

questions.provingSentenceText: Each book weighed twenty pounds and took minutes to trace just one sentence with a finger.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 1 that tells how much each book weighed and how long it took to trace one sentence.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 explicitly states that the wax-coated books weighed twenty pounds each and took minutes just to trace a single sentence with a finger.

questions.prompt: Part A: Why did Louis Braille's six-dot cell allow people to read much faster than Captain Barbier's twelve-dot code?

options.text: The six-dot cell only had enough patterns for the first ten letters of the French alphabet.
The smaller six-dot cell fit under one fingertip at once, so readers could glide smoothly across the page.
The six-dot bumps glowed in the dark so soldiers could see them from across a room.
The six-dot cell was printed on twenty-pound wax pages that never wore down.

questions.provingSentenceText: A reader could now glide smoothly across a page without stopping.
questions.childTip: Check the end of Paragraph 3 to see what happened once the whole six-dot cell fit under a fingertip in one touch.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that Barbier's twelve-dot cell required moving the finger up and down on every symbol, whereas Braille's six-dot cell could be felt in a single touch, letting readers glide smoothly across the page.
